metadata.title: Gate-Behavior Test Harness: A Gate Is Not a Vote

beats.narration_text: Nik Bear Brown. Build it with a CLI, then take it apart.

beats.role_note: the stakes BEFORE the build begins — no terminal yet
beats.narration_text: Most scoring pipelines claim to have gates. A gate — the real thing — zeros the composite when it trips. No partial credit, no dampening, no weighted deduction. But most pipelines implement a vote dressed as a gate: the dead posting shaves forty points off the composite, and the candidate with the highest score sometimes wins a job that no longer exists. A single pytest fixture tells the two apart — and it runs red before you fix the scorer, green after. This video shows you how to write it.
beats.visual_intent: title card: 'gate vs vote — the job that doesn't exist'; PROBLEM beat, no terminal yet

build.suggested: suggested prompt: Most scoring pipelines claim to have gates. A gate zeros the composite when it trips. A dead posting scores forty-two on the vote implementation.

beats.narration_text: In the terminal: ask Claude to write a pytest suite for a job-scoring function that must treat two conditions as hard gates — posting live being false, and months to start exceeding the OPT window. Three fixtures: a live role that passes, a dead posting that must be zeroed, a role past the OPT window that must be zeroed. Include one intentionally wrong gate-as-vote implementation and show the suite failing on it, then the correct gate implementation passing.

props.command:
claude "Write a pytest suite for score(role)
with two hard gates:
  posting_live==False → score must be 0
  months_to_start>opt_window → score must be 0
Three fixtures: live+in-window; dead posting;
past OPT window. Assert score()==0 on gate fail.
Include a gate-as-vote implementation (will fail)
and a correct gate implementation (will pass)."

beats.role_note: terminal (Onda) — read the output before running
beats.narration_text: Read the critical lines before running. The gate implementation has one shape: if posting underscore live is false, return zero immediately — not score minus forty, not score times zero-point-three, zero. And the test assertion has one shape: assert score of dead equals exactly zero. Not less than ten. Not less than threshold. Equals zero. Both lines together state the behavioral contract more precisely than any documentation.

Run pytest on the vote implementation first. The dead-posting fixture fails: score returns forty-two, the assertion expects zero, the test turns red. Now swap in the gate implementation. Run again. All three fixtures pass. Green. The test didn't change — the dead job still has the same data. The only thing that changed is whether zero is enforced or approximated.
beats.visual_intent: screen-recording: pytest run on vote scorer → red (dead posting returns 42, not 0); swap implementation → pytest run on gate scorer → green; one assertion line highlighted

props.code:
$ pytest gate_behavior_test.py -v

# --- vote implementation ---
FAILED test_dead_posting_is_zero
  AssertionError: assert 42 == 0

# --- gate implementation ---
PASSED test_live_role_scores_positive
PASSED test_dead_posting_is_zero
PASSED test_past_opt_window_is_zero

3 passed in 0.04s

beats.role_note: terminal (Onda) — extend to unknown gate state
beats.narration_text: Now the harder case: liveness is not false, it's unknown — the liveness checker errored, returned nothing. Ask Claude to add a fourth fixture where posting underscore live is None and assert the scorer raises ValueError rather than guessing. A scorer that treats unknown liveness as true is worse than one that refuses to score.

props.command:
claude "Add a fourth fixture to gate_behavior_test.py:
posting_live=None (checker errored, not empty).
Assert score() raises ValueError — refuse to
score on unknown gate state. Show a 'guess True'
implementation failing the new fixture."

beats.narration_text: A gate that doesn't fail loudly isn't a gate — it's a vote with a better name. The test formalizes the difference in nine lines: the assertion is equals zero, not less than threshold, not less than ten. Write the test before the scorer and it specifies the behavior faster than any design document. And the unknown-state fixture is the test the vote implementation will always miss: 'I couldn't check' is not the same as 'it passed.'
beats.visual_intent: recap card: 'gate == 0 enforced; vote ≈ 0 approximated'; the one assertion line as a static code block

build.suggested: suggested prompt: A gate that doesn't fail loudly isn't a gate. Write the test before the scorer. The assertion is == 0, not < threshold.

beats.narration_text: Your move: find the hardest gate in your pipeline. Write the fixture that fails on a vote implementation first — before you touch the scorer. If you can't write the failing test, you don't yet know what your gate is supposed to do. That gap in your knowledge is more valuable to find now than after the pipeline ships.
beats.visual_intent: next-steps card: 1) find the hardest gate, 2) write the failing fixture first, 3) fix the scorer to make it pass
